svg.text: Moment of inertia, angular momentum and its conservation

g.text: F = m a_T = m r alpha -> r F = tau = m r^2 alpha
tau_total = (sum m_i r_i^2) alpha = I alpha (3.18)
I = sum m_i r_i^2 (3.19)
tau = I alpha is the rotational analogue of F = ma: I plays the
role of mass; it depends on m and on its distance from the axis
thin rod I = (1/12) m L^2
hoop I = m r^2
disc I = (1/2) m r^2
sphere I = (2/5) m r^2

svg.text: wider one has the greater I

g.text: L = r x p (3.20); L = r p sin theta = m r v sin theta
circle: theta = 90, L = m r v = m r^2 omega
rigid body: L = (sum m_i r_i^2) omega = I omega
unit kg m^2 s^-1 = J s; L is perpendicular to the plane of r and p,
by the right-hand rule, along the axis of rotation with omega;
a particle has angular momentum about an axis if its angular
position changes relative to that axis
L_total = L1 + L2 + ... = constant
I1 omega1 = I2 omega2
if no external torque acts on a system, its total
angular momentum stays constant: verified from
the cosmological to the sub-microscopic level
the axis of rotation keeps its orientation unless
an external torque changes it: the Earth's axis
stays fixed relative to the universe
diver: curls up, I falls, omega rises; stretches
out before entry, I rises, omega falls (Fig. 3.18)
skater: arms and leg in, I small, omega large;
out, I large, omega small (Fig. 3.19)
turntable: pulling the dumb-bells in raises
the angular speed (Fig. 3.20)

svg.text: Flywheel, gyroscope, Example 3.5 and the side notes

g.text: flywheel (Fig. 3.21): a heavy wheel on an axle; stores rotational energy, smooths output fluctuations and gives stability in bicycles and
vehicles, industrial machinery, gyroscopes, ships and spacecraft; its angular momentum resists changes of orientation; the balance wheel
regulates mechanical clocks and watches by keeping a controlled rate of oscillation
gyroscope (Figs. 3.22, 3.23): a mounted flywheel pivoted in supporting rings; spinning fast it has a large angular momentum L = I omega, so
changing the direction of its axis needs a large torque; a tilted gyroscope keeps levitated without falling; used in the guiding systems of
aeroplanes, submarines and space vehicles to hold a direction in space
Example 3.5: Earth, m = 6.00 x 10^24 kg, orbit radius r = 1.50 x 10^11 m, one revolution in 3.16 x 10^7 s: v_o = 2 pi r / t, so
L_o = m v_o r = 2 pi r^2 m / t = 2 pi (1.50 x 10^11)^2 (6.00 x 10^24) / (3.16 x 10^7) = 2.67 x 10^40 kg m^2 s^-1; positive because the revolution is counter-clockwise
side notes: a moving bicycle stays upright because the spinning wheels' angular momentum resists change; a ball on a string wrapping round a
finger speeds up as its radius shrinks; a coasting rotating funnel slows as water drips into a beaker (Point to Ponder); melting polar ice flowing
away as rivers raises the Earth's moment of inertia, so its angular velocity falls and the day lengthens; planets in elliptical orbits speed up
when nearer the Sun (conservation of angular momentum, Point to Ponder)
